title: Design exercise: metrics and time series pipeline
summary: A classic design exercise: a metrics system for tens of millions of series with dashboards, alerts and tiered retention. The reference answer sizes the sample stream from stated assumptions and the Gorilla compression figure, decouples ingestion from storage with a samples log, keeps a compressed 26-hour window in memory, compacts into immutable blocks with downsampled tiers, narrows queries through an inverted index, and treats cardinality as the unit of capacity with hard per-tenant limits.

exercise.prompt: Design the metrics system for a company's services: thousands of instances emit counters, gauges and histograms every few seconds, engineers query the last few hours on dashboards and alerts, and a few people need a year of history at coarser resolution. The system must not fall over when one team adds a label that explodes into millions of series.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Ingest metrics by scrape and by push; store them with labels; answer range and instant queries over labels with aggregation functions; evaluate alerting rules; enforce per-tenant series limits.
Raw data for 15 days; minute aggregates for 90 days; hour aggregates for 15 months.
20,000 service instances, each exposing 2,000 series, so 40 million active series; a 15 s scrape interval.
chosen for the exercise; derive the sample rate, the raw and compressed volumes and the hot-window memory yourself
50 tenants (teams); 500 dashboard and rule queries per second at peak, most over the last hour.
A sample is queryable within 30 s of being scraped; a last-hour query answers in under 1 s at p99 and a 30-day query in under 10 s.
99.9 percent availability for ingestion and for alert evaluation; no single tenant can degrade another's ingestion.
Logs and traces (separate systems that share label conventions), anomaly detection, billing, the dashboard product itself.

clarifying_questions.a: A metric name plus a unique set of label key-value pairs; every distinct combination is a separate stream of (timestamp, value) samples, which is the Prometheus data model.
Pull by default (the scraper controls the rate and knows when a target is down); push for batch jobs and for edge locations that cannot be scraped, through a gateway that applies the same limits.

A label must never carry an unbounded value (user ids, request ids, full URLs); the Prometheus instrumentation guidance says to keep a metric's label cardinality small, below about 10 as its rule of thumb, because every label set is a separate series, and the ingest layer enforces a per-tenant series limit with rejection and an alert when it is hit.

clarifying_questions.q: How exact must old data be?
clarifying_questions.a: Downsampled: for data older than 15 days, 1-minute aggregates (min, max, sum, count) are enough; older than 90 days, 1-hour.

Classic histograms are counted as bucket series plus sum and count. The example's 20 buckets include the +Inf bucket, so it counts 22 series; native histogram storage is not included in this float-sample model.

clarifying_questions.q: Can a query span all tenants?
clarifying_questions.a: No; queries are tenant-scoped, with a platform tenant that may read everything for fleet-level views.

blocks.text: Every number below follows from the stated assumptions: 20,000 instances exposing 2,000 series each, a 15 s scrape interval, and the compression figure the Gorilla paper reports. The tables carry the arithmetic; the paragraphs carry the assumptions.

blocks.caption: Rates and daily volumes derived from the assumptions.
rows: 20,000 instances times 2,000 series; classic histogram bucket counts include +Inf, plus sum and count
40 million series every 15 s; scraping is flat, there is no daily peak
16 bytes per sample, an 8-byte timestamp and an 8-byte float, the figure Gorilla starts from
1.37 bytes per sample, the Gorilla average for delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR values, a 12x reduction
20,000 targets every 15 s; a live scraper emits up=0 when its target fails. A dead scraper emits nothing.
dashboards and rules at peak, most over the last hour (assumption)
500 queries times a few hundred series each over one hour, 240 samples per series; a memory-bound scan, not a disk one

blocks.caption: Sizes: the hot window, the tiers and the index.
rows: Compressed samples: 320 GB/day times 26/24, plus 4 GB of series headers under the stated header-size assumption.
two replicas of the window: a few dozen large nodes, or more small ones
320 GB per day times 15, in object storage
four values (min, max, sum, count) a minute instead of one every 15 s is about the same bytes per series per day as raw; 320 GB times 90 (assumption: no further compression counted)
320 GB/day divided by 60 times 450 days; months are 30 days. All retention tiers overlap from the present.
instead of 172,800 raw samples; the reason the tiers exist

blocks.text: Series count is a useful capacity unit at a fixed scrape interval and retention, not a substitute for bytes. In this model retained samples dominate headers; the header-size assumption is 100 bytes per series, 4 GB for 40 million series. Cardinality limits bound both sample traffic and per-series overhead; query fan-out and churn still require separate measurement. Gorilla's compression figure is an observed average, not a guarantee for these metrics.

Scrapers pull targets on a schedule (the Prometheus model) and a push gateway accepts what cannot be scraped; both go through an ingest layer that validates labels and enforces per-tenant series limits before anything is stored. Samples land on a partitioned log keyed by series hash, which decouples ingestion from storage and lets the hot store be rebuilt. The hot store keeps the last 26 hours in memory, compressed, replicated twice; a compactor writes 2-hour blocks to object storage and downsamples into tiers. A query frontend splits a query by time range, caches results, and fans out to hot shards and long-term blocks.

blocks.legend: Boxes separate ingestion, storage and queries. The log decouples writes, but restart safety requires full-window block hydration plus tail replay before serving. Retention and checkpoint-lag bounds apply; a bare checkpoint cannot restore lost memory.

blocks.text: Three published systems have this shape. Gorilla at Facebook is a write-through in-memory cache of the most recent 26 hours in front of a durable store, compressing samples to 1.37 bytes on average. Monarch at Google has a regionalised architecture, keeps the data in memory, and pushes query evaluation down as close to the source data as possible. Uber's M3 puts a coordinator in front of the storage nodes that handles downsampling, retention and rollup rules per subset of metrics.

blocks.text: The write path through AWS, part a: a scrape, its validation against the tenant's limit, and the append to the stream.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant T as Target
  participant SC as Scraper
  participant IN as Ingest
  participant DDB as Registry
  participant K as Kinesis
  SC->>T: GET metrics
  alt target responds
    T-->>SC: samples
  else live scrape fails
    SC->>SC: create up=0 sample
  end
  SC->>IN: retryable sample batch
  IN->>DDB: transact series and quota
  alt quota rejected
    DDB-->>IN: quota conflict
    IN-->>SC: explicit rejection
  else existing or created series
    DDB-->>IN: canonical series ids
    IN->>K: PutRecords aggregates
    K-->>IN: per-record results
    loop failed records only
      IN->>K: retry same sample identities
      K-->>IN: per-record results
    end
    IN-->>SC: ack durable records only
  end
blocks.legend: Scraper sharding is this design's choice. The producer retains unacknowledged batches and checks every PutRecords result, including HTTP-success partial failures. Acknowledged samples are not intentionally dropped. Consumers deduplicate by tenant-qualified series and timestamp, reject conflicting values explicitly and accept late samples into correction blocks rather than assuming stream order. The registry creation transaction atomically claims metadata, posting lists and quota. Sources: partitioning s8, aggregation s10, endpoint s11 and conditions s25; these are primitives, not an exactly-once claim.

blocks.text: The physical log is larger than timestamp-plus-value samples: the chosen representation and headers produce about 87.4 MB per second. We provision 120 shards for byte throughput and two standard readers, with headroom subject to benchmarking.

Each sample carries a tenant-qualified series fingerprint plus timestamp and value; labels live in the registry. Producers pack samples for the same physical shard and flush on a size or time boundary. Partial aggregates and retries increase charges beyond the full-batch model, so the cost table states that assumption explicitly.
Part b: the hot store consumes its shards and the compactor writes the blocks, with the two failures that matter: a lost hot task and a compactor that falls behind.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 14
  participant K as Kinesis
  participant HOT as Hot store
  participant CP as Compactor
  participant S3
  alt replacement task
    HOT->>S3: GetObject window manifest
    S3-->>HOT: blocks and durable checkpoint
    HOT->>S3: GetObject full window blocks
    S3-->>HOT: retained samples and index
  else running task
    Note over HOT: keep serving current replica
  end
  HOT->>K: GetRecords after checkpoint
  K-->>HOT: records
  HOT->>HOT: deduplicate and insert by time
  HOT-)CP: closed chunks
  CP->>S3: PutObject blocks then manifest
  S3-->>CP: durable manifest checkpoint
  CP-->>HOT: durable frontier
  Note over HOT: serve only after catch-up
blocks.legend: The application checkpoint lives in an immutable S3 manifest published after every referenced block is durable. It advances only across contiguous stream records represented in those blocks, including late-sample correction blocks. A replacement hydrates the entire hot window, not just the tail, then replays newer records. The chosen default stream retention is sufficient only while checkpoint lag plus catch-up stays below its retention horizon; alarm and backpressure well before that boundary. If exceeded, declare an unrecoverable gap rather than fabricating samples. No extended retention is priced. Sources: retention s9, replacement s17, compression s2 and S3 access s23.

  participant QF as Query frontend
  participant S3 as S3 blocks
  participant RE as Rule evaluator
  participant SNS
  opt older subrange needed
    QF->>S3: GetObject index and chunks
    alt objects available
      S3-->>QF: older partial result
    else unavailable
      S3-->>QF: error
      Note over QF: mark result partial
    end
  end
  QF-->>Q: merge recent and older
  RE->>QF: evaluate rule
  QF-->>RE: result
  RE->>SNS: Publish with alert identity
  SNS-->>RE: accepted
  Note over RE,SNS: duplicates remain possible
blocks.legend: The response follows both subranges. SNS and replicated evaluators provide at-least-once notification attempts, not exactly one notification; the decision guide s13 gives at-least-once delivery for HTTP/S endpoints. Every alert includes tenant, rule, labels and evaluation-window identity so an idempotent downstream receiver can suppress duplicates; receivers without that contract may see duplicates. Sources: S3 endpoint s23, SNS s32 and delivery guarantees s13.

blocks.text: Nothing in the read path writes to the stream or to S3; the only writes are the cache fills. A query that would touch more series than its tenant's limit is refused before any shard is called, which is the read-side half of the cardinality rule.

blocks.caption: The samples log: Kinesis provisioned, Kinesis on-demand, Amazon MSK, or SQS.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, provisioned shards
rows.pick_when: the throughput is known and flat, consumers need per-key ordering and replay, and the producer can aggregate records
rows.avoid_when: the load swings by an order of magnitude within a day, so sized shards sit idle or throttle
rows.example: For this design: chosen with a measured-throughput requirement. The cost model includes series identity and aggregation headers, and restores replacement tasks from full-window blocks before log catch-up.

rows.pick_when: the throughput is unknown or bursty and nobody wants to count shards; it scales from a few MB per second to many GB per second in this Region
rows.avoid_when: a flat, high volume billed per GB written and read costs many times the equivalent shards
rows.example: For this design: not chosen at the assumed steady load. The physical aggregate model with both hot replicas reading costs about $33,800 monthly on demand, including the fixed stream-hour charge.

rows.pick_when: the team already runs Kafka clients, wants its ecosystem and compression, or needs retention and partition counts beyond what a managed stream offers
rows.avoid_when: a small team with no Kafka estate, where brokers to size, patch and rebalance buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: a legitimate alternative to benchmark. Three small brokers cost $446.76 in compute alone, not an equivalent total: replicated storage, client compression and measured ingest/read throughput must also be sized.

rows.pick_when: one consumer, idempotent work, no ordering and no replay, and the simplest hand-off
rows.avoid_when: consumers need order per key, replay from a position, or several readers of the same data
rows.example: For this design: not chosen because multiple replicas need retained-log replay positions. Queue-side ordering or deduplication does not reconstruct a lost in-memory window.

blocks.caption: The hot store and the services: ECS on Fargate, ECS on EC2, EKS, or Lambda.

rows.pick_when: steady, container-shaped services, including stateful ones whose memory fits the largest task size and whose state can be rebuilt from a log
rows.avoid_when: a shard needs more memory than one task offers, local NVMe, or a particular instance family
rows.example: For this design: chosen for everything. The hot store's shard replicas fit a Fargate task of 16 vCPU and 120 GB, with eight of them holding the 700 GB window; the scrapers, ingest, compactor, frontend and evaluator are plain stateless tasks scaled on lag and request rate.

rows.pick_when: the memory per shard exceeds the task maximum, or the hot store wants local NVMe for spill and faster restarts, or reserved instances make a steady fleet cheaper
rows.avoid_when: the team wants no instances to patch and the task sizes suffice
rows.example: For this design: compare a measured EC2 fleet against eighty hot replicas at the larger scale, matching the cost table's headroom. Larger memory instances may reduce task count, but savings and recovery throughput require measurement.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes, wants its operators for stateful sets, or portability across clouds
rows.avoid_when: a handful of services and no Kubernetes estate; the cluster fee, the upgrade cadence and the SRE time buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen, though a stateful set is the shape many open-source metrics stores ship as; the ECS service scheduler and the log replay give the same recovery without the cluster to run.

rows.pick_when: event-shaped, short, stateless work with spiky volume, paid per request
rows.avoid_when: long-lived state in memory, held connections, or a flat high volume where per-request billing dwarfs the compute
rows.example: For this design: not chosen anywhere on the hot path; a hot store is the opposite of stateless, and the scrapers run continuously.

blocks.caption: The long-term store, the index, and the buy option: S3 and DynamoDB, Timestream, or the managed Prometheus service.

rows.option: Amazon S3 for the blocks, Amazon DynamoDB for the registry
rows.pick_when: the long-term data is immutable blocks read by range, and the index is key lookups at a modest write rate
rows.avoid_when: the long-term queries need a query engine over the raw points rather than block reads
rows.example: For this design: chosen. Blocks are written once and read by time range, the cheapest shape object storage serves; the registry maps a series to its shard and counts series per tenant with conditional writes, which is a key-value workload.

rows.pick_when: the team wants a managed time series database with a memory store and a magnetic store, SQL over the points, and no compactor to run
rows.avoid_when: the data model is Prometheus series and PromQL, and the hot path is an in-memory window the team controls
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Its memory and magnetic tiers mirror this design's hot window and blocks, but the query language and the series model differ from what the dashboards and rules speak.

rows.pick_when: the team wants the Prometheus data model and PromQL without running ingestion, storage or querying, and its volume sits in the cheaper tiers
rows.avoid_when: the volume is tens of millions of series, where the per-sample price tiers add up to far more than the equivalent fleet
rows.example: For this design: the buy option. Ingestion alone is about $116,000 at the stated volume; the comparison excludes operational staffing on both sides. A smaller workload needs its own self-managed sizing and managed bill, not a categorical recommendation.

rows.option: A relational or wide-column store for the points
rows.pick_when: relational joins matter, or a wide-column series/time-range access pattern and existing operational expertise fit
rows.avoid_when: a measured alternative cannot meet retention, scan or ingestion needs economically
rows.example: For this design: object blocks plus a hot cache are a choice, not proof that wide-column storage is unsuitable. Wide-column is a valid series/time alternative requiring its own compaction and query plan.

blocks.caption: The results cache: ElastiCache for Valkey, in-task memory, ElastiCache Serverless, or DAX.

rows.pick_when: the cache is shared by all frontend tasks, the working set is small and steady, and a replica covers a node loss
rows.avoid_when: the working set swings widely or is tiny enough to live in each task
rows.example: For this design: chosen, one small node with a replica. Dashboards repeat the same queries every refresh, so a shared cache of sub-range results turns most of the 500 queries a second into cache hits; a lost primary fails over to the replica.

rows.pick_when: each frontend task can hold the working set and a miss is cheap
rows.avoid_when: many tasks each miss the same query, so the shards do the work many times over
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Six frontend tasks would each warm the same buckets; the shared cache does it once.

rows.pick_when: the working set is unpredictable and nobody wants to size nodes
rows.avoid_when: a small, steady working set where one node and a replica cost less than the per-GB-hour charge
rows.example: For this design: not chosen; the working set is a few gigabytes held all day.

rows.pick_when: the cache fronts a DynamoDB table and the reads are item lookups
rows.avoid_when: the cached values are query results, not table items
rows.example: For this design: does not apply; the cached objects are evaluated sub-ranges, not registry items.

blocks.caption: The design reviewed against the six Well-Architected pillars and the Data Analytics Lens.
columns: what it asks of this design
rows: observability for actionable insights; anticipate failure; frequent, small, reversible changes
the observability system watches itself: ingest lag, rejected samples per tenant, oldest unflushed chunk and query p99 by tier as the alarms; ECS rolling deployments; a game day for a lost hot task
the metrics about the metrics system live in the same system; a separate small alarm on ingestion is the only outside check
a strong identity foundation; least privilege; protect data in transit and at rest; keep people away from data
one task role per service; tenant scoping on every query; the push listener and the query listener on the only public entry; encryption at rest and in transit
residual risks include tenant-filter bugs, credential compromise and unsafe label ingestion; security priority does not make those risks disappear
automatically recover from failure; scale horizontally; stop guessing capacity
two replicas across zones; durable full-window blocks and manifest followed by log-tail catch-up; ECS replacement and hard active-series quotas
replacement hydrates the entire hot window before replaying after its durable checkpoint; the other replica serves alone during recovery
consider mechanical sympathy; go global in minutes where it fits
compressed samples and shard-local evaluation; retained label index narrows history too. The literal mixed-resolution monthly query scans 62.5% of the all-raw points, not a quarter.
the largest Fargate task bounds the shard size; beyond it the hot store moves to instances
adopt a consumption model; measure overall efficiency; analyze and attribute expenditure
cost per million series on the dashboard and charged back per tenant; provisioned shards for a flat load; the managed service priced as the buy option and rejected on its tiers at this volume
a fleet sized for the window is paid all month; a reservation would cut it once the series count is proven steady
maximize utilization; use managed services; align to demand
Arm tasks; inactive series leave hot memory and active quota, while labels remain discoverable through retained history; downsampled tiers reduce old sample bytes
the hot window is held in memory twice; a single copy would halve the memory and double the blast radius
general analytics workload best practices, applied here as an author's design review
our choices are decoupled ingestion, resolution tiers and tenant showback; the landing page does not prescribe these protocols
the specific recovery and quota protocols still require implementation review and measurement

blocks.text: The hot store is the largest line, but not most of this corrected subtotal. Registry transactions and the physical log are material costs. Compression, retention, replica count and bounded cardinality all affect capacity; production measurements must include the named overhead exclusions.

blocks.caption: Entities.
rows: series_id, tenant, canonical name/labels, active flag, generation, last_seen, inactive_at; identity hash includes tenant
tenant-qualified series identity; verify canonical labels on hash collisions
Prometheus defines a series by name and labels; tenant qualification and collision checks are this platform's isolation choices.
stored as compressed chunks of about 120 samples (assumption) per series in the hot tier, delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR values
tenant, from, to, resolution (raw, 1m, 1h), series index, chunk files
immutable, in object storage; each block carries its own inverted index
retained tenant label lists and canonical metadata, independent of active quota
DynamoDB PK tenant#label#value#bucket, SK series_id; bounded buckets and tenant#series metadata keys

Query/intersect every relevant bucket including inactive identities, then fetch metadata and requested block ranges. Labels survive until all retained tiers have expired. Regex needs a bounded vocabulary scan or rejection.
tenant_id, active_series, max_series, max_samples_per_second, retention overrides
tenant_id counter and tenant-qualified series keys

Creation atomically writes metadata, five label items and active-counter increment. Deactivation changes metadata and decrements the counter once, without deleting discovery. Reactivation increments quota conditionally and advances generation. Historical collection deletes metadata/labels only after the inactive retention deadline and a generation/state check.
replicated evaluation; alert identity accompanies at-least-once notifications, with deduplication at capable receivers

blocks.caption: This platform's chosen API, inspired by Prometheus; the overview is not a specification of these endpoint semantics.
rows: a range of samples per matching series
split by time at the tier boundaries, cached per (tenant, query, step, time bucket)
answered from the index without touching chunks
a batch of samples with labels
the push gateway's endpoint; the same limits as the scrape path

blocks.text: The query language is a label-selector-and-function language in the PromQL shape; the exercise does not design it. Rules are declared in files per tenant and evaluated through the same query path as dashboards.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: One scrape cycle, one compaction, and one dashboard query; the step numbers run on across the three parts.
Part a: a scrape and its ingestion, with the limit that protects the other tenants.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant T as Target
  participant SC as Scraper
  participant IN as Ingest
  participant IX as Series index
  participant LOG as Samples log
  SC->>T: scrape
  alt target responds
    T-->>SC: samples
  else live scrape fails
    SC->>SC: up=0 observation
  end
  SC->>IN: retryable tenant batch
  IN->>IX: atomic series and quota claim
  alt quota rejected
    IX-->>IN: rejected
    IN-->>SC: explicit error
  else identity available
    IX-->>IN: canonical identity
    IN->>LOG: append physical aggregates
    LOG-->>IN: per-record durable results
    IN-->>SC: acknowledge durable samples
  end
blocks.legend: Consistent-hash scraper assignment is this design's choice, not a claim from the Prometheus overview s1. Unacknowledged records are retried with stable sample identities; consumers deduplicate and handle late timestamps explicitly. A dead scraper emits no samples. Cardinality guidance comes from s5/s6.

blocks.text: Part b: the hot store consumes the log and the compactor turns closed chunks into blocks and tiers.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 12
  participant LOG as Samples log
  participant HOT as Hot store
  participant CP as Compactor
  participant LT as Long-term blocks
  opt replacement task
    HOT->>LT: load full-window manifest
    LT-->>HOT: blocks and checkpoint
  end
  HOT->>LOG: read after durable checkpoint
  LOG-->>HOT: tail records
  HOT->>HOT: deduplicate and insert by time
  HOT-)CP: closed chunks and frontier
  CP->>LT: write blocks then manifest
  LT-->>CP: durable frontier
  CP-->>HOT: checkpoint may advance
blocks.legend: Full-window hydration precedes tail replay. The checkpoint advances only when durable blocks cover its contiguous records, including corrections for out-of-order samples. Compression follows Gorilla s2; the block duration is our design choice. M3 s4 supports downsampling/retention rules, not this exact block duration or recovery protocol.

blocks.text: Part c: a last-hour dashboard query, and the rule evaluator that uses the same path.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 21
  participant Q as Dashboard
  participant QF as Query frontend
  participant IX as Retained discovery index
  participant HOT as Hot shards
  participant LT as Long-term blocks
  Q->>QF: range query
  QF->>IX: retained tenant label lists
  IX-->>QF: live and inactive series ids
  QF->>HOT: recent subrange
  HOT-->>QF: partial result
  opt older range
    QF->>LT: matching index and chunks
    LT-->>QF: older result or error
  end
  QF-->>Q: merged result, partial flag
  Note over QF: alerts use this same query path
blocks.legend: Historical discovery does not depend on active-series membership: labels and canonical identity outlive every retained sample tier. The frontend discovers inactive series too, then reads the selected blocks. This retention protocol is our design; shard-side evaluation is supported by Monarch s3 and alert practice by s7.

blocks.text: Cardinality multiplies both metadata and sample traffic: an unbounded user-id label can create millions of series. At fixed scrape interval and retention it is a useful quota unit, but this worked window is dominated by retained sample bytes, not its headers. Enforce atomic active-series quotas, sample-rate limits and bounded query fan-out, and report the labels responsible for growth.

Cardinality guidance limits unbounded labels; active quota bounds the hot window, not the lifetime history index. Deactivation is serialized against renewal/reactivation, releases active quota once and leaves canonical labels discoverable. After admission closes and outstanding accepted records are drained, record inactive_at; retain discovery for the longest sample horizon after that instant. Any reactivation invalidates collection through its generation condition. Active-lease/last-seen refresh operations are not included in the churn-only cost subtotal.

Historical discovery retention is 460 days after deactivation, conservatively covering the 15-month hourly tier; tenant overrides cannot exceed that modeled horizon without resizing. Active series retain metadata indefinitely. A collector removes the six discovery items only when metadata is still inactive at the expected generation and its deadline has passed. Delayed collection adds storage, never causes an early loss of discoverability.

blocks.title: Why the tiers exist: one 30-day query
items: A 30-day dashboard panel asks for one series over 30 days.
At raw resolution that is 172,800 samples per series (one every 15 s).
At the 1-minute tier it is 43,200 points, a quarter of the raw count, and the panel cannot show more anyway.
A literal split at the 15-day boundary reads 86,400 recent raw samples plus 21,600 older minute points. Returning 43,200 minute points requires resampling the recent portion too.
A fleet-level query over every tenant never runs ad hoc at full resolution: the platform tenant reads pre-aggregated recording rules.

blocks.text: Reads scale by narrowing before scanning: the inverted index turns a label selector into a small set of series and the shards that hold them, the frontend splits long ranges into cached sub-ranges, and pushing aggregation down to the shards keeps the data where it is, which is Monarch's main argument.
Each row names the failure, what engineers see, and the mitigation.

blocks.caption: Failure modes.
rows: its series are unavailable for recent queries until the replica serves them
hydrate the entire hot window from durable raw S3 blocks, restore its manifest checkpoint, then replay later log records with deduplication; do not expose the shard until caught up
consumers scale on lag; ingestion keeps accepting; alert on lag over 30 s
that tenant's new series are rejected
per-tenant enforcement at ingest; other tenants unaffected; counted errors and a cardinality report
hot tier cannot drop old data; memory grows
scale or repair compaction and apply ingestion backpressure before memory exhaustion. Increasing the window increases memory pressure. Never discard acknowledged data silently.
long-range queries fail; recent queries fine
query frontend returns partial results with a flag; compactor retries; the 26-hour window covers the common case
its targets have missing or stale samples, not new up=0 values
reassign targets to live scrapers; preserve gaps. Only a live scraper observing target failure emits up=0.

reference_answer.title: Trade-offs and the alternative not taken

blocks.text: The decisions a reviewer reads first.

blocks.caption: Trade-offs.
rows: push everything versus pull by default with a push gateway
the scraper knows when a target is down and controls the rate; push for what cannot be scraped
disk-based store for everything versus an in-memory compressed window
most queries are recent; compression may make memory affordable, but the paper's observed average must be measured on this workload
scrapers write straight to the store versus a samples log in between
backpressure, rebuilds and replays; storage nodes can restart without losing scrapes
a year of raw data is about 120 TB compressed (320 GB per day) for nothing most queries need
best effort versus hard per-tenant limits
one tenant must not take the system down; the limit is the capacity unit

blocks.caption: The numbers at 10x.
rows: two replicas; regional hot tiers with a global query layer, Monarch's zones
hot-store partitions per tenant, so a noisy tenant is confined to its shards
quotas and showback measured in active series and in query cost
ad hoc fleet queries at full resolution are refused
a published cost per million series per month

blocks.text: At this scale, changes to sample representation and trace correlation are platform decisions: define compatibility, quota accounting and query semantics before changing the storage model. Do not infer a new series identity or a fixed compression factor from a feature name.

blocks.caption: Physical representation and billing assumptions, not measured compression or fleet guarantees.
rows: 16-byte tenant-qualified series fingerprint, 8-byte timestamp, 8-byte value: 32 bytes. Canonical labels remain in the registry.
2,000 samples plus 1,536 bytes for framing/partition overhead fit a 64-KiB record. Pack by physical shard; flush within 100 ms.
Each full record uses three 25-KiB PUT units. Full packing produces about 1,333 records/s and 4,000 PUT units/s.
Both hot replicas read every record. On-demand comparison includes ingress plus two reads and one stream-hour charge.
Default stream retention only. Full-window hydration uses retained raw blocks; tail catch-up must finish before uncheckpointed records expire. Alarm and backpressure before that boundary.

Seven items on first creation, two on deactivation, six on eventual historical collection; transactional doubling gives 30 write units per distinct churn lifecycle. Assume 4M distinct replacements daily.

Each serialized metadata, label-index or counter item fits one KiB including attribute names/keys; the six discovery items together fit two KiB in this priced model. Larger labels require rejection or rounded-up capacity, not the same price.
40M active plus 4M daily distinct inactive identities retained for 460 days: 1.88B identities at steady state.

Budget 5,000 billed GB for retained discovery and counters at base; tenfold storage at larger load. This covers the two-KiB identity bound plus the per-item storage overhead that DynamoDB billing adds, with headroom.
One strong metadata read per newly encountered identity, below four KiB. Historical selector reads, active refreshes, reactivations and retry/collection-lag overhead are excluded.
Teaching volumes are decimal. Budget the numeric total as 36,000 AWS billed GB conservatively rather than claim equality with binary units. Larger tier uses the actual 51,200-GB breakpoint.
30 request-days, 730 running hours. Tenfold task and shard counts are unbenchmarked sizing assumptions.

blocks.text: Hot memory remains the largest line, not a majority. Retained historical discovery, transactional churn and the physical log are material costs. Gorilla reports observed average compression, not a fixed ratio. Publish cost per active series together with retention/churn assumptions; active quota alone does not bound historical index growth.

L1: Scrape and push ingestion, a time series store with labels, a query API and tiered retention.
The sample rate (2.7 million per second) and raw volume derived from the stated assumptions, with the compressed figure cited.
A per-tenant series limit enforced at ingest, with the cardinality rule stated.
L2: The in-memory hot window with compression, a samples log between ingestion and storage, and 2-hour immutable blocks with an inverted index.
Downsampling tiers and query splitting with a results cache; fan-out to the shards narrowed by the index with pushdown of aggregation.
Replicated rule evaluation and the up=0 convention so absence is visible.
Series churn and the memory-per-series argument as the capacity model.
L3: A multi-tenant metrics platform: regional zones with federation, tenant isolation of partitions, quotas and showback per series and per query.
Cost per million series per month as the number the platform is held to, and recording rules as a necessity at fleet scale.
What the system refuses: unbounded labels, cross-tenant ad hoc queries, dropping hot data before blocks are durable.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: what a series is, pull versus push, the cardinality rule, downsampling, histograms, tenant scoping. Say the numbers aloud: 40 million series, 2.7 million samples per second, 43 MB per second raw and about 3.7 MB per second compressed, a 26-hour hot window of about 700 GB with two replicas.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Series, Sample in compressed chunks, Block with an inverted index, Tenant limits, Rule; the query and series endpoints and the push write endpoint.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: scrapers and push gateway, ingest with limits, the samples log, the hot store, compactor and tiers in object storage, the query frontend. Say what the log buys.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: cardinality as the capacity unit (limits, reports, churn, memory per series), then the query path (index narrowing, splitting and caching, downsampled tiers, pushdown, replicated rules).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x platform (zones and federation, isolation, showback), and the L3 sentence: the unit of capacity is a series, not a byte, and the design is about who may create one.

Context and scope: The services and their instrumentation today, the dashboards and alerts that depend on it, the outage or cost that motivates a new system, and the label conventions shared with logs and traces.
Goals and non-goals: Freshness within 30 s, last-hour queries under 1 s, tiered retention, tenant isolation; logs, traces, anomaly detection and the dashboard product out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: ingestion with limits, the samples log, the hot tier, compaction and tiers, the query frontend and rules.
Alternatives considered: Push everywhere, a disk-based store for everything, direct writes without a log, raw retention forever, best-effort cardinality, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security (tenant scoping on every query, who may change limits), observability of the observability system (ingest lag, rejected samples per tenant, compaction backlog, query p99 by tier, rule evaluation lag), cost per million series per month, rollout by scraping both systems for a tenant and comparing.
Review questions the doc must answer: What happens on the day a tenant doubles its series in an hour, and what a dashboard shows while object storage is unavailable.
